items.prompt: The French Advance chain: White's d4 and e5 face Black's d5 and e6. Black to move: find the pawn move that attacks the base of White's chain.

claims.statement: White's d4 is the base of its chain.
After c5 a black pawn attacks d4.
c5 and Bd7 are within 40 centipawns of the engine's best move.

hints: The base is the rearmost pawn of the chain: the one nothing protects.
Which black pawn move would attack d4?
A pawn from the c-file.
items.explain: d4 is the base of White's chain (it protects e5 and no pawn protects it). The pawn move ...c5 attacks it. The engine rates c5 within 40 centipawns of its best move, so this lever is sound here.

feedback_by_move.c8d7: A sound developing move (within 40 centipawns of the best), but it is not the pawn lever against the base.

items.prompt: Same chain, White to move after ...c5. Find a move that gives the base d4 a second defender.

claims.statement: After c3 White has two defenders of d4.
After Nf3 White has two defenders of d4.
Now White has one defender of d4.
c3 and Nf3 are within 40 centipawns of the engine's best move.

hints: Count what defends d4 now.
A pawn or a piece can add the second defender.
Two natural moves do it: one pawn move, one knight move.
items.explain: d4 has one defender now (the queen). Both c3 and Nf3 add a second, and both are within 40 centipawns of the engine's best. The family plan for the chain's owner: keep the base defended while playing on the wing the chain points to.

items.prompt: Game C (a tournament game from 1916). Black to move. Again the chain: find the pawn move that attacks the base of White's chain.

claims.statement: After c5 a black pawn attacks d4.
c5 is the engine's best move.

hints: It is the same structure as before.
Which pawn can attack d4?
The c-pawn.
items.explain: The same lever as in Game A, in a game played about a century earlier: ...c5 attacks the base d4, and the engine ranks it first here. The structure, not the date or the move order, tells you the plan.

items.prompt: Game A (an online game from January 2013, both players rated about 2100). White to move. White's chain still stands. In the game White played g4 here. Which plan class does g4 belong to?

answer.class: play on the wing the chain points to
options: hit the base of the chain
hit the head of the chain
play on the wing the chain points to
gain space on the other wing

claims.statement: g4 is the engine's best move.
After g4 a white pawn stands on the g4 square, on the kingside.
White's e5 pawn is protected by a pawn.

hints: Which way does the chain d4-e5 point?
The head e5 points toward the kingside.
g4 pushes pawns on that wing.
items.explain: The chain d4-e5 points toward the kingside, and g4 starts pawn play on that wing; the engine ranks g4 first here. The label 'play on the wing the chain points to' is the lesson's name for this plan, a rule of thumb rather than a theorem.

items.prompt: Game B (an online game from January 2013, players rated about 2100 and 1800). Black to move. In the game Black played c4 here, a pawn move that is not an attack on d4. Which plan class does it belong to?

answer.class: gain space on the other wing
options: hit the base of the chain
hit the head of the chain
play on the wing the chain points to
gain space on the other wing

claims.statement: After c4 a black pawn attacks b3.
After c4 a black pawn attacks d3, where White's bishop stands.
Nxd4, cxd4 and c4 are all within 40 centipawns of the engine's best move.

hints: Black's chain points toward the queenside.
c4 does not attack d4. It cramps White on the wing where Black has pawns.
A family holds more than one plan.
items.explain: c4 takes space on the queenside and attacks b3 and d3, instead of capturing on d4. Three Black moves, including this one, are within 40 centipawns of each other, so the family has more than one sound plan. The label is the lesson's name for it [I].

items.prompt: Black to move in the French Advance chain. Does the plan 'hit the base of the opponent's chain with a pawn' apply here?

claims.statement: White's d4 is the base of its chain.
White's e5 is protected by a pawn.
After c5 a black pawn attacks d4.

hints: Is there a chain, with a base that no pawn protects?
d4 protects e5 and nothing protects d4.
A pawn lever can attack it.
items.explain: The chain is there (e5 protected by d4, d4 unprotected by pawns) and a pawn can attack the base. The family plan applies.

items.prompt: Game C (a tournament game from 1916). Black to move on move 12. Does the plan 'hit the base of White's chain with a pawn' still apply?

claims.statement: A black pawn stands on d4: White's d4 pawn is gone.
No white pawn is protected by a pawn: the chain has gone.

hints: Is White's d4 pawn still there?
A black pawn stands on d4 now.
No white pawn is protected by another pawn.
items.explain: Black captured on d4 earlier in the game, so the chain is gone: no white pawn is protected by a pawn, and a black pawn stands where the base was. The plan 'hit the base' now has nothing to hit. A game that has left its structure is read on its own.

items.prompt: A game with no pawn chain: White to move. Does the plan 'hit the base of the opponent's chain with a pawn' apply to either side?

claims.statement: No white pawn is protected by a pawn.
No black pawn is protected by a pawn.

hints: Is any pawn protected by another pawn?
Look at both sides.
Neither side has a chain.
items.explain: No pawn on either side is protected by a pawn, so there is no chain and no base. The family never applied here, and the question is not 'wrong' but empty. Other structures bring other plans.

items.prompt: Game C (a tournament game from 1916). White to move. White's chain stands. In the game White played Qg4 here. Which plan class does it belong to?

answer.class: play on the wing the chain points to
options: hit the base of the chain
hit the head of the chain
play on the wing the chain points to
gain space on the other wing

claims.statement: Qg4 and h4 are within 40 centipawns of the engine's best move.
After Qg4 the queen attacks the pawn on g7.

hints: Which way does the chain point?
Toward the kingside.
Where does the queen go, and what does it attack?
items.explain: The queen goes to the kingside, where the chain points, and attacks g7. Qg4 and h4 are both within 40 centipawns of the engine's best, so this plan holds up in the 1916 game too.

answer.class: the two moves are within 40 centipawns of each other
options: the two moves are within 40 centipawns of each other

claims.statement: e5 and exd5 are within 40 centipawns of the engine's best move.

hints: The engine compares the two moves by a number.
How far apart are the numbers?
Closer than 40 centipawns.
items.explain: The engine puts the two moves within 40 centipawns of each other, so it neither confirms nor refutes the annotator's preference: a gap that small is a difference of taste. The old verdict is neither right nor wrong by this number; what the annotator knew and wanted is a separate question.

items.prompt: Game C (a tournament game from 1916; the annotator is the player of the black pieces, writing in 1921). Black to move on move 24. The annotator wrote that f5, which Black played, was not the best move. Does today's engine rank it the way the annotator did?

Far lower.
items.explain: The engine rates f5 at least 50 centipawns below its first choice, so engine and annotator agree that it was not the best. Where an old remark and today's number agree, the check is cheap and the remark gains a little weight.

items.prompt: Game C (a tournament game from 1916; the annotator is the player of the black pieces, writing in 1921). White to move on move 15. claims.statement: Rd1 is the engine's best move.

It is the engine's first choice.
The annotator talked about plans, the engine gives a number.
items.explain: The engine ranks Rd1 first, so it disagrees with the annotator's verdict. But the remark was about a plan (an attack that White gives up), and one number does not measure that. Do not settle it by the number alone: say what each source is measuring.
